newsitem.title: GERMANY: Europe past EMU point of no return - Rexrodt.
newsitem.headline: Europe past EMU point of no return - Rexrodt.

text.p: Europe has crossed the point of no return in its drive to establish a single currency, and now has no choice other than to create the Euro in 1999 as planned, German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said on Monday.
"The point of no return has been crossed," he told a forum on European economic and monetary union (EMU).
Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, at the same event, emphasized the gravity of the situation as EU members prepared to make economic union irrevocable by abandoning individual currencies.

Tietmeyer said stability must be ensured over the long run, and he warned against possible attempts by members to "window-dress" their economic data to be sure of making the grade for the launch of the Euro currency in January 1999.

In a thinly-veiled reference to Britain, Tietmeyer also attacked the policies of some European countries who seemed determined only to select the best aspects of Europe's planned monetary union, rejecting the common currency goal.
Tietmeyer made clear in his address that countries which want to join the Euro project must do more than simply meet on-paper targets for economic criteria in 1997.

"The European Monetary Institute (EMI) should not and will not let itself be blinded by one year's results. This is not a question of window-dressing, but rather of solidity. It is a question of durability and sustainability," he said.

Rather it was essential for the success of EMU that all countries taking part from the start showed the same commitment to fiscal discipline, which will be monitored by the EMI -- the future European central bank.
"That is why the choice of participants who fit together is such a central point. Success or failure hinges on this to a decisive extent," he said.
He defended the need for precise limits on economic performance in order to qualify for currency union, but said this should not lead to a "naive faith" in the numbers.

Turning to a controversy within the European Union about a planned inter-central bank payments system, Tietmeyer repeated the German central bank's view that central banks excluded from EMU should have only limited access to the system, known as TARGET.
Britain has objected in strong terms to plans to limit London's access to the planned wholesale payments system for the Euro, but Tietmeyer said: "It is not just or sensible to treat unlikes alike."
The Bank of England believes plans to limit its access to intra-day, interest-free Euro credits will unfairly disadvantage London as a financial centre.
Germany counters that no central bank anywhere else in the world has a right to create cash in another currency and that this could undermine the stability of the Euro.
Tietmeyer added that it had to be made clear that countries could not pick and choose what they wanted from the array of advantages the new single currency, the Euro, will bring.

Britain's ruling Conservative Party is deeply divided over its European policy, with a fociferous section of the parliamentary group determined the country should stick to its option to stay out of monetary union.

With policy options for struggling economies within the EMU group set to be very limited, German industry associations warned at the forum that the labour market would have to cushion the economy against external shocks.

"When exchange rates are fixed, a buffer against real economic shocks is removed. The corrective function of exchange rates will have to be taken by greater flexibility, particularly in the labour market," said 16 organisations led by the Federation of German Industry (BDI).
